topic: What is chemistry? The science of everything around you
notes: Episode 1 of a beginner chemistry series. Hook with everyday chemistry (cooking, soap, rusting, breathing). End by teasing the next video on matter.
must_include: chemistry studies matter and how it changes; three everyday examples

topic: What is matter? Anything with mass that takes up space
notes: Beginner series. Viewers know nothing yet. Show what is and isn't matter (air is matter; light and sound are not).
must_include: mass; volume; air has mass

topic: Solid, liquid and gas: the three states of matter
notes: Explain using particle pictures: how tightly particles are packed and how they move.
must_include: particle arrangement in each state; shape and volume of each

topic: Melting, boiling, freezing and condensing: how matter changes state
notes: Use water as the running example. Heat gives particles energy. Keep sublimation as a one-line bonus.
must_include: melting point and boiling point of water (0 and 100 degrees Celsius at sea level)

topic: Physical change vs chemical change: how to tell them apart
notes: Everyday examples: melting ice, tearing paper vs burning paper, cooking an egg, rusting.
must_include: a new substance forms in a chemical change; signs of a chemical change

topic: Elements, compounds and mixtures explained simply
notes: Use simple examples: oxygen (element), water (compound), salt water and air (mixtures).
must_include: fixed ratio in compounds; mixtures can be separated physically

topic: How to separate mixtures: filtration, evaporation and distillation
notes: Show each method with a kitchen-style example. Distillation in one clear diagram.
must_include: which method suits which mixture

topic: What is an atom? The tiny building block of everything
notes: Give a sense of scale (how small an atom is) with one memorable comparison. Atoms make up elements.
must_include: atoms are mostly empty space

topic: Inside an atom: protons, neutrons and electrons
notes: Nucleus in the centre, electrons around it. Charges and rough relative masses.
must_include: charge of each particle; electrons are far lighter

topic: Atomic number and mass number: the two numbers of every element
notes: Use carbon and sodium as examples. Show how to count protons, neutrons and electrons from the two numbers.
must_include: neutrons = mass number minus atomic number; worked example

topic: Isotopes: same element, different weights
notes: Carbon-12 vs carbon-14 and hydrogen's isotopes. One real use (carbon dating or medicine).
must_include: same protons, different neutrons

topic: How electrons are arranged in shells: the 2, 8, 8 rule
notes: Show shell filling for the first 20 elements with 2-3 worked examples (oxygen, sodium, calcium). Say it is a simplified model for beginners.
must_include: K, L, M shells; electronic configuration of sodium 2,8,1

topic: Valence electrons: why atoms react with each other
notes: Atoms want a full outer shell. Link to the shells video. Noble gases already have one.
must_include: valence electrons; the octet idea

topic: From Dalton to Bohr: how scientists discovered the atom
notes: Timeline of atomic models: Dalton, Thomson (plum pudding), Rutherford (gold foil), Bohr (shells). Dates must be accurate.
must_include: year and big idea of each model

topic: What is the periodic table and how is it organised?
notes: Rows are periods, columns are groups. Elements are in order of atomic number. Why the shape looks odd.
must_include: 118 elements; periods and groups

topic: Mendeleev: the man who left gaps for elements nobody had found
notes: The story of Mendeleev's table and his predicted elements (such as eka-silicon, later germanium).
must_include: predicted elements were later discovered

topic: Metals, non-metals and metalloids: where they sit on the periodic table
notes: The zig-zag staircase line. Properties of each kind with everyday examples.
must_include: properties of metals vs non-metals; examples of metalloids

topic: Alkali metals: why sodium and potassium react so violently with water
notes: Group 1. Explain with one valence electron. Reactivity increases down the group. Safety: never try at home.
must_include: one valence electron; reactivity increases down the group

topic: Halogens: the salt-making elements of group 17
notes: Fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine. Uses: chlorine in water treatment, iodine in iodised salt.
must_include: seven valence electrons; reactivity decreases down the group

topic: Noble gases: why helium and neon refuse to react
notes: Full outer shell. Uses: balloons, neon signs, argon in bulbs.
must_include: full outer shell; real uses

topic: Periodic table trends: why atoms get bigger and smaller
notes: Atomic size across a period and down a group, explained with shells and the pull of the nucleus.
must_include: size decreases across a period, increases down a group

topic: Memorise the first 20 elements in 60 seconds with a mnemonic
notes: Teach one catchy mnemonic sentence for H to Ca in order, in chunks of 5, with a quick recall at the end. Make it fun.
must_include: all 20 symbols in order: H He Li Be B C N O F Ne Na Mg Al Si P S Cl Ar K Ca

topic: Element symbols that don't match their names: Na, K, Fe, Au and more
notes: Explain the Latin names behind them, with a memory hook for each.
must_include: Na sodium, K potassium, Fe iron, Cu copper, Ag silver, Au gold, Sn tin, Pb lead, Hg mercury

topic: Memorise the periodic table groups with stories
notes: A short mnemonic or story for group 1, group 2, the halogens and the noble gases. Different from the first-20 mnemonic.
must_include: one memory hook per group

topic: The memory palace trick for learning the periodic table
notes: Explain the method of loci as a walk through a house, placing elements as funny images. Show it with the first 10 elements.
must_include: how the memory palace works; worked example with the first 10 elements

topic: Learn valency the easy way: a trick using group numbers
notes: How valency comes from valence electrons; the trick for groups 1, 2 and 13-17. A simple note on exceptions.
must_include: valency of common elements (H, O, N, C, Na, Cl, Mg)

topic: How to memorise the whole periodic table: a complete method
notes: A longer guide combining chunking, mnemonics, the memory palace, spaced repetition and quick self-tests. Don't repeat the earlier short mnemonic videos word for word; build a full study plan.
must_include: a 7-day revision plan; how to test yourself

topic: Ions: why atoms gain or lose electrons
notes: Sodium loses one electron, chlorine gains one. Positive and negative ions.
must_include: cation and anion; Na+ and Cl-

topic: Ionic bonding: how table salt holds together
notes: Electron transfer from sodium to chlorine and the attraction between the ions. Properties of ionic compounds.
must_include: electron transfer; high melting point of ionic compounds

topic: Covalent bonding: atoms that share electrons
notes: Water, hydrogen and methane as examples. Single and double bonds.
must_include: shared electron pairs; water molecule H2O

topic: Metallic bonding: why metals conduct electricity
notes: The sea of electrons model. Why metals are shiny, bendable and conduct heat and electricity.
must_include: sea of delocalised electrons

topic: How to read a chemical formula like H2O and CO2
notes: What the letters and small numbers mean. Count the atoms in H2O, CO2, H2SO4 and Ca(OH)2.
must_include: subscripts; brackets multiply

topic: Writing chemical formulas with the criss-cross method
notes: Use valency to write formulas: sodium chloride, magnesium oxide, aluminium oxide, calcium chloride.
must_include: criss-cross steps; Al2O3 worked example

topic: What is a chemical reaction? Reactants, products and equations
notes: Word equation, then symbol equation, with burning magnesium or methane as the example.
must_include: reactants on the left, products on the right

topic: Law of conservation of mass: atoms are never lost
notes: Lavoisier's idea. Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed. Sets up balancing equations.
must_include: total mass before equals total mass after

topic: How to balance chemical equations step by step
notes: Two worked examples: H2 + O2 to H2O, then CH4 + O2. Only change the big numbers in front, never the subscripts.
must_include: coefficients vs subscripts; balanced 2H2 + O2 = 2H2O

topic: Four types of chemical reactions with everyday examples
notes: Combination, decomposition, displacement and double displacement, one example each.
must_include: one balanced example per type

topic: Exothermic and endothermic reactions: heat out vs heat in
notes: Burning and respiration vs photosynthesis and instant cold packs.
must_include: energy released or absorbed

topic: Oxidation and reduction: what rusting and burning have in common
notes: Oxidation as gain of oxygen or loss of electrons, reduction as the opposite. Rusting and corrosion as examples.
must_include: the OIL RIG memory trick

topic: Acids and bases explained: from lemon juice to soap
notes: Everyday acids and bases, how they taste and feel (safety: never taste lab chemicals). Introduce H+ and OH- simply.
must_include: common household acids and bases

topic: The pH scale: from battery acid to drain cleaner
notes: 0 to 14, 7 is neutral. Place everyday substances on the scale.
must_include: pH of pure water is 7; acids below 7, bases above 7

topic: Natural indicators: turmeric, litmus and red cabbage
notes: How indicators change colour in acids and bases; turmeric turns red with soap or other bases.
must_include: litmus colours in acid and base; turmeric with a base

topic: Neutralisation: when an acid meets a base
notes: Acid + base gives salt + water. Real uses: antacids for acidity, treating insect stings, treating acidic soil.
must_include: acid + base = salt + water; one balanced example

topic: The mole: how chemists count atoms
notes: Introduce the mole as a counting unit like a dozen. Avogadro's number. Molar mass of water as the example.
must_include: 6.022 x 10^23; molar mass of H2O is 18 g/mol

topic: What makes reactions faster? The five factors
notes: Temperature, concentration, surface area, catalysts and pressure for gases. Everyday examples (food in a fridge, crushed vs whole tablets).
must_include: collision theory in one line
